comment: The error was solely C versus D: zero-decay Adagrad achieved lower CE than its otherwise identical wd=1e-4 twin. I supplied an unsupported regularization tie-break. At lr=1e-4, Adagrad’s progress proxy is only 2·lr·√512≈0.00453; coupled decay can perturb both the learning gradient and its accumulator without providing a useful generalization benefit. This is a plausible mechanism, not a measured explanation. K1002 and K1070 helped rank the optimizer groups. K1005 explicitly warned against universal decay tie-breaks; the KB did not justify my C-first decision. Matched backtests favor lower decay in 17/17 historical pairs, but only 4/6 lab pairs; both lab reversals are higher-progress XOR comparisons.
hypothesis:
Candidate rule: For default-initialized networks trained with Adagrad, when model, dataset, loss, learning rate and budget match exactly, T≤1024 and 2·lr·√T≤0.01, prefer lower coupled weight decay among tested values from 0 through 0.001.

Mechanism hypothesis: In this low-progress regime, decay-induced changes to gradients and accumulated squared gradients can impair early task fitting; meaningful overfitting reduction is less likely to compensate. This predicts D<C here, without changing A<E<B.

Historical backtest, excluding this question: 6 eligible decay-only pairs across 6 questions, 6 hits and 0 misses. These cover bigram, spiral, multivariate and univariate tasks, but no XOR instances. The lab contains no eligible matched low-progress pairs. Across all matched Adagrad lab decay comparisons, lower decay wins 4/6; the two misses share one XOR16 dataset at T1024 and lr=.001/.003, outside the proposed progress scope.

Thus this is a falsifiable cross-task tie-break candidate, not an established XOR law. Fresh matched XOR8 controls at T512, lr=.0001, wd=0 versus .0001 are needed to test transfer.
